content: The effects of diffraction at the limits of depth of field (DOF) become significant only when using relatively large f-numbers. However, large f-numbers typically necessitate longer exposure times, which often result in motion blur that causes a greater loss of sharpness than diffraction itself. The interplay between defocus and diffraction has been explored in detail in works such as Hansma (1996), Conrad's Depth of Field in Depth, and Jacobson's Photographic Lenses Tutorial. Post-capture image manipulation is not considered in this context. Techniques like deconvolution or unsharp masking can enhance the perceived DOF in the final image, especially when the original image already has a large DOF. Conversely, noise reduction techniques can diminish the apparent DOF. For digital imaging using color filter array sensors, the process of demosaicing is also excluded from this analysis. Demosaicing typically reduces the effective DOF, although some algorithms may incorporate sharpening, which could counteract this effect. Lens designers cannot limit their analysis to Gaussian optics alone and must account for lens aberrations. However, the practical requirements of photography are less stringent than those of lens design. Despite the simplifications inherent in most DOF formulas, these formulas have proven effective in determining camera settings that yield acceptably sharp images. It is important to note that DOF limits are not rigid boundaries between sharp and unsharp regions, and there is little value in calculating these limits to an excessive degree of precision. DOF vs. Format Size To a first approximation, DOF is inversely proportional to the size of the camera format. More precisely, if photographs with the same final image size are taken using two different camera formats at the same subject distance, field of view, and f-number, the DOF is inversely proportional to the format size. This relationship holds true when the subject distance is large compared to the focal length but small compared to the hyperfocal distance for both formats. This approximation is generally useful for comparing results across different formats. To maintain the same field of view, the focal lengths of the lenses must be proportional to the format sizes. For example, if a 4×5 format camera uses a 300 mm lens, a 35 mm camera would require a 75 mm lens to achieve the same field of view. At the same f-number, the image captured with the 35 mm camera would have four times the DOF of the image captured with the 4×5 camera. In many cases, the desired image dictates the required DOF. For a given DOF and field of view, the necessary f-number is proportional to the format size. For instance, if a 35 mm camera requires f/11, a 4×5 camera would need f/45 to achieve the same DOF. At the same ISO speed, the exposure time for the 4×5 camera would be sixteen times longer than that for the 35 mm camera. For example, if the 35 mm camera requires 1/250 second, the 4×5 camera would require 1/15 second. In windy conditions, the longer exposure time of the larger camera might result in motion blur. Adjusting the f-number to match the camera format is equivalent to maintaining the same absolute aperture diameter. The greater DOF of the smaller format can be either an advantage or a disadvantage, depending on the desired effect. For the same amount of foreground and background blur, a smaller-format camera requires a smaller f-number and allows for a shorter exposure time than a larger-format camera. However, many point-and-shoot digital cameras cannot achieve a very shallow DOF. For example, a small-format camera with an f/8 aperture has the same DOF as a 35 mm camera with a normal lens at f/13. In some scenarios, camera movements such as tilt or swing can be employed to better align the DOF with the scene, achieving the required sharpness at a smaller f-number. Photolithography In semiconductor photolithography, DOF is critically important because integrated circuit layout features must be printed with extreme precision at very small scales. The challenge lies in the fact that the wafer surface is not perfectly flat and may vary by several micrometers. Even such small variations can distort the projected image, leading to unwanted deviations in the resulting pattern. To address this, photolithography engineers take extraordinary measures to maximize the optical DOF of the equipment. Additionally, chip manufacturers like IBM use chemical mechanical polishing machines to further flatten the wafer surface before lithographic patterning. Digital Techniques for Increasing DOF Focus Stacking Focus stacking is a digital image processing technique that combines multiple images taken at different focus distances to produce a final image with a greater DOF than any of the individual source images. Software programs such as PhotoAcute Studio, Helicon Focus, and CombineZM are available for multi-shot DOF enhancement. Achieving sufficient DOF can be particularly challenging in macro photography. The images on the right illustrate the increase in DOF that can be achieved by combining multiple exposures. Wavefront Coding Wavefront coding is a method that convolves light rays in such a way as to produce an image where all fields are simultaneously in focus, with all planes out of focus by a constant amount. Plenoptic Cameras A plenoptic camera employs a microlens array to capture four-dimensional light field information about a scene. Derivation of the DOF Formulas DOF Limits A symmetrical lens is illustrated on the right. The subject at distance (s) is in focus at image distance (v). Point objects at distances (D_mathrm{F}) and (D_mathrm{N}) would be in focus at image distances (v_mathrm{F}) and (v_mathrm{N}), respectively. At image distance (v), they are rendered as blur spots. The DOF is controlled by the aperture stop diameter (d); when the blur spot diameter equals the acceptable circle of confusion (c), the near and far DOF limits are at (D_mathrm{N}) and (D_mathrm{F}).
